title: Study of Acids, Bases and Salts
tagline: Indicators, the pH scale, neutralisation and the four families of salts — with the laboratory prep each one asks for.

overview.intro: This unit collects the ideas students use in every practical paper: what makes a substance acidic or basic, how indicators show it, how the pH scale measures it, and how neutralisation turns an acid and a base into a salt. The salt family matters as much as the definition, because exam questions routinely ask for the preparation, one property and one use of a named salt. Learn the pattern — acid plus what gives which salt — and every variation becomes predictable.

facts.label: Acid behaviour
facts.value: Produces hydrogen ions as the only positive ion when dissolved in water.

facts.label: Base behaviour
facts.value: Produces hydroxide ions in water; an insoluble base is called an alkali only when soluble.

facts.label: Neutralisation
facts.value: Acid + base gives salt + water, with the release of heat.

facts.label: pH scale
facts.value: Runs 0 to 14; below 7 acidic, exactly 7 neutral, above 7 basic.

learningOutcomes: Define acids and bases in the water sense and distinguish a base from an alkali.
Name and describe the colour change of at least four indicators in acid and in base, including the pH range each covers.
Explain the pH scale and relate hydrogen ion concentration to acidity, including dilution effects.
Classify salts as normal, acid, basic or double and give the reacting combination that prepares each type.
Describe the laboratory preparation of a named salt, including crystallisation and the role of water of crystallisation.

learn.title: What counts as an acid and what counts as a base

blocks.text: In the water sense used at this level, an acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions as the only positive ion when it dissolves in water, while a base is a substance that produces hydroxide ions. A base that dissolves in water is called an alkali, so every alkali is a base but not every base is an alkali: copper(II) oxide is a base and is insoluble, whereas sodium hydroxide is a soluble base and therefore an alkali. The same substance can also be classified by oxide behaviour. Acidic oxides such as carbon dioxide react with alkalis to give salts, basic oxides such as sodium oxide react with acids, and amphoteric oxides such as aluminium oxide and zinc oxide react with both, which is why they dissolve in either hydrochloric acid or sodium hydroxide.

items: An acid releases H+ in water; the H+ never exists alone but attaches to water as the hydronium ion.
A base neutralises an acid to give a salt and water; an alkali also turns red litmus blue.
Metallic oxides are mostly basic; non-metallic oxides are mostly acidic; amphoteric oxides such as Al2O3, ZnO and PbO react with both.
A strong acid such as hydrochloric acid ionises almost completely; a weak acid such as ethanoic acid ionises only partly.

items.note: HCl molecules split almost completely into H+ and Cl-, giving a high hydrogen ion concentration.

items.text: Zinc oxide dissolving in sodium hydroxide
items.note: The amphoteric oxide forms a zincate ion, showing that it also behaves as an acidic oxide.

items.meaning: A base that dissolves in water, such as sodium hydroxide or aqueous ammonia.
An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases, such as aluminium oxide.
An acid that ionises completely in water, such as hydrochloric acid.
Reaction of an acid with a base to form salt and water with the release of heat.

blocks.text: An indicator is a substance whose own colour depends on whether the solution around it is acidic or basic. Litmus is the oldest: red in acid, blue in base. Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base, which makes it useful near pH 4, while phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base, useful near pH 9. Methyl red changes around pH 5, and thymol blue covers two ranges, so a single drop of it can show weak acidity, neutrality and basicity in turn. Universal indicator or pH paper gives a colour for every whole pH value, turning the single yes-or-no question into a scale reading. Choosing the right indicator matters because a titration must end where the neutralisation actually ends, not before it.

items: Litmus: red in acid, blue in base; it is the test named in the syllabus for both directions.
Methyl orange: red in acid, yellow in base; suited to strong acid versus weak base titrations.
Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in base; suited to strong base versus weak acid work.
Universal indicator gives a full colour scale, so pH 1 reads deep red and pH 13 reads deep blue.

items.text: Adding phenolphthalein to dilute sodium hydroxide
items.note: The solution turns pink immediately, showing a base before any titration begins.
An orange colour near pH 3 shows a weak acid rather than a strong one.

learn.title: The pH scale and what moves it

blocks.text: The pH scale converts hydrogen ion concentration into a single number between 0 and 14. A pH below 7 is acidic, exactly 7 is neutral, and above 7 is basic; each whole step represents a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration, so pH 3 is a hundred times more acidic than pH 5. Pure water at 25 °C reads 7 because the ionisation of water produces equal numbers of hydrogen and hydroxide ions. Adding acid raises the hydrogen ion count and lowers pH; adding alkali lowers the hydrogen ion count and raises pH; diluting an acid moves pH upwards towards 7 without ever crossing it. The scale also explains why very strong acids sit near 0 and why body fluids such as blood stay close to 7.4, where enzyme chemistry works.

items: pH = 7 neutral, pH < 7 acidic, pH > 7 basic; the scale is logarithmic, not linear.
Diluting an acid by a factor of ten raises its pH by one unit.
Rainwater is slightly acidic because dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid.
A buffer resists pH change; blood uses a carbonate buffer to stay near 7.4.

items.text: Hydrochloric acid at pH 1 against ethanoic acid at pH 3
items.note: Both are acids, but the strong acid releases far more hydrogen ions per molecule.

items.text: Adding a drop of alkali to a buffered solution
items.note: The pH hardly moves because the buffer absorbs the added hydroxide ions.

items.meaning: Negative logarithm to base ten of the hydrogen ion concentration in a solution.
Solution with pH 7 at 25 °C, where hydrogen and hydroxide ion concentrations balance.
System that resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.

learn.title: Neutralisation and the families of salts

blocks.text: Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base to give salt and water, and the choice of the second reactant decides the kind of salt produced. Acid plus soluble base gives a normal salt directly; acid plus metal oxide or metal carbonate also gives a normal salt, with carbon dioxide fizzing off in the carbonate case. If only part of the replaceable hydrogen of an acid is neutralised, an acid salt results, such as sodium hydrogen sulphate. If a metal hydroxide is only partly neutralised, a basic salt results, such as basic copper carbonate or lead hydroxide chloride. Double salts form when two salts crystallise together, and the alum family is the standard example. This single pattern — how many hydroxides or hydrogens are involved — answers most classification questions.

items: Normal salt: all replaceable hydrogen of the acid replaced, as in NaCl from HCl and NaOH.
Acid salt: partial neutralisation of a polyprotic acid, as in NaHSO4.
Basic salt: partial neutralisation of a polyacidic base, containing OH or O alongside the salt.
Double salt: two salts sharing one crystal lattice, such as potassium alum, which ionises to give three kinds of ion.

items.text: Sodium chloride from sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid
items.note: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O, an exothermic reaction used as the standard neutralisation.

items.text: Carbon dioxide passed into lime water
items.note: It turns milky because calcium carbonate precipitates, then clears in excess as soluble hydrogen carbonate forms.

blocks.caption: Which combination gives which salt
rows: Alum from aluminium and potassium sulphates

learn.title: Preparing a pure salt and reading its crystals

blocks.text: The standard laboratory preparation of a soluble salt has four steps: dissolve the insoluble base or carbonate in warm acid until no more dissolves, filter off the excess, evaporate the filtrate until a crystallising film appears, then cool slowly so crystals grow. Slow cooling gives large, regular crystals because the ions have time to settle into the lattice; rapid cooling gives a powder. Crystals that form from water often hold water inside the lattice, the water of crystallisation. Blue copper sulphate crystals carry five water molecules and turn to a white powder when gently heated, and the colour returns when water is added — a reversible change that proves the water is chemically held, not merely wet. A salt that has lost its water of crystallisation is said to be anhydrous.

items: Use excess insoluble reactant so that all the acid is used up and the filtrate contains only the desired salt.
Evaporate to a film, not to dryness, otherwise the crystals are contaminated with any dissolved impurity.
Cool the solution slowly to obtain well-formed crystals rather than a fine crust.
Heating blue copper sulphate crystals above about 100 °C drives off water and leaves anhydrous white copper sulphate.

items.note: Warm copper(II) oxide in dilute sulphuric acid, filter, evaporate to a film, cool slowly and filter off blue crystals.
Anhydrous copper sulphate stays white if a sample is truly dry and turns blue only when water is present.

items.meaning: Fixed number of water molecules held inside the crystal lattice of a salt.
Containing no water of crystallisation, as in white copper sulphate powder.
Thin crust on the surface of an evaporating solution showing it is ready to cool.

keyPoints: An acid gives hydrogen ions as the only positive ion in water; a base gives hydroxide ions.
An alkali is a soluble base; every alkali is a base, but insoluble bases such as copper oxide are not alkalis.
Litmus is red in acid and blue in base; phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base.
pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is basic, and each unit is a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.
Neutralisation is acid plus base giving salt and water, and it releases heat.
Normal, acid, basic and double salts differ by how much of the acid hydrogen or base hydroxide is replaced.
Preparing a soluble salt: react excess solid with warm acid, filter, evaporate to a film, cool slowly.
Water of crystallisation is water held in the lattice; blue copper sulphate loses it on heating and regains it on wetting.
Amphoteric oxides such as aluminium oxide and zinc oxide dissolve in both acids and alkalis.
Strong acids ionise completely; weak acids ionise partly, which is why equal concentrations give different pH values.
examFocus: Learn the indicator chart as a small table; colour-change questions are direct marks every year.
For a pH question, state the direction of change first: adding acid lowers pH, diluting acid raises it towards 7.
Salt preparation answers must name all four steps in order, including the reason for filtering and the reason for slow cooling.
When asked to identify a salt family, count how many replaceable hydrogens or hydroxides were involved before naming the type.

vocabulary.meaning: A base soluble in water, producing hydroxide ions in solution.
Measure of hydrogen ion concentration on a logarithmic scale from 0 to 14.
Reaction between an acid and a base forming salt and water.
Water molecules held in fixed positions inside a crystal lattice.
Able to react with both acids and bases, as aluminium oxide does.
Salt formed by partial neutralisation of the replaceable hydrogen of an acid.
Substance that changes colour according to whether the solution is acidic or basic.

questions.prompt: Phenolphthalein added to a dilute sodium hydroxide solution turns:
questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base, and sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali.

questions.prompt: Which oxide would dissolve in both dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: Zinc oxide is amphoteric, so it reacts with acids and with alkalis, while the others are acidic or basic only.

questions.prompt: A solution with a pH of 3 compared with one of pH 6 is:
questions.explanation: Each pH unit is a tenfold difference, so three units make 10 × 10 × 10, a thousandfold difference.

questions.prompt: The salt formed when only part of the replaceable hydrogen of sulphuric acid is neutralised is called a:
questions.explanation: Partial neutralisation of an acid leaves some replaceable hydrogen, which is exactly an acid salt such as NaHSO4.

questions.prompt: A base that dissolves in water is called an __________.
questions.explanation: Solubility in water is the only difference between a base and an alkali.

questions.prompt: The fixed number of water molecules held in a crystal lattice is called the water of __________.
questions.explanation: The water is part of the lattice structure, so heating removes it and changes the crystal form.

questions.prompt: Define an acid in terms of the ions it produces in water.
questions.answer: An acid produces hydrogen ions as the only positive ion when dissolved in water, together with a corresponding negative ion.
questions.explanation: This water-based definition covers both mineral acids such as HCl and organic acids such as ethanoic acid.

questions.prompt: Explain why methyl orange is a poor choice for titrating a weak acid against a strong alkali.
questions.answer: Methyl orange changes colour between about pH 4 and 6, while the equivalence point of a weak acid with a strong alkali lies above pH 7, so the indicator would change far too early and the titration would end before neutralisation was complete.
questions.explanation: The indicator range must contain the pH at which neutralisation actually ends.

questions.prompt: What change is observed when blue copper sulphate crystals are heated strongly?
questions.answer: The blue crystals lose water of crystallisation and become a white anhydrous powder, and steam is given off.
questions.explanation: Heating drives the lattice water away; adding water again restores the blue colour.

questions.prompt: Describe how pure copper sulphate crystals are prepared from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulphuric acid, giving the reason for each step.
questions.answer: Excess copper(II) oxide is warmed with dilute sulphuric acid until no more dissolves, so that all the acid is used and the solution contains only copper sulphate. The mixture is filtered to remove the unreacted solid. The filtrate is evaporated until a crystallising film appears, because evaporating to dryness would leave impurities behind. The solution is then cooled slowly, so that crystals grow large and regular, and the blue crystals are filtered off and dried between filter papers. The product is hydrated copper sulphate holding five molecules of water in each formula unit.
questions.explanation: Excess solid removes the acid, filtering removes solid, partial evaporation keeps the salt in solution, and slow cooling gives pure large crystals.

questions.prompt: Classify each of the following and justify your choice: sodium chloride, sodium hydrogen sulphate, lead hydroxide chloride, potassium alum.
questions.answer: Sodium chloride is a normal salt because all the replaceable hydrogen of hydrochloric acid has been replaced by sodium. Sodium hydrogen sulphate is an acid salt because only one of the two hydrogens of sulphuric acid has been replaced. Lead hydroxide chloride is a basic salt because a hydroxyl group from the base remains in the lattice. Potassium alum is a double salt because it crystallises from a mixture of two salts and yields potassium, aluminium and sulphate ions in solution.
questions.explanation: The family is decided by how much of the acid hydrogen and base hydroxide remains in the crystal.

questions.prompt: A colourless solution reads pH 2 on universal indicator. On diluting it tenfold the reading changes to 3, and adding one drop of alkali barely changes it. Explain both observations.
questions.answer: A tenfold dilution reduces the hydrogen ion concentration tenfold, and since pH is a logarithmic measure that raises the pH by exactly one unit, from 2 to 3. The small change on adding alkali indicates a buffer: the added hydroxide ions are absorbed by the buffering system rather than raising the hydroxide concentration, so the pH stays close to its original value. Neither observation takes the solution past neutrality, because dilution approaches pH 7 asymptotically and a trace of alkali cannot neutralise a strong acid.
questions.explanation: Logarithmic pH explains the one-unit shift, and resistance to added base is the defining behaviour of a buffer.
